NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Lemon Beebrush, then Lemon Verbena) and matches its page-title parenthetical; the record leads with Lemon Verbena because RHS's dedicated page leads with it (the subtitle beneath its H1, and its page title Aloysia citrodora | lemon verbena) and NC State's Description opens with Lemon verbena.
records.toxicity_detail: Scope is only NC State's structured Problems field, which lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses; the page's tag list separately carries #problem for cats, #problem for dogs and #problem for horses. NC State carries no Poisonous to Humans block for this species: no Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle, Causes Contact Dermatitis or Poison Part field appears, so the source gives no severity, symptom, poison part or toxic principle, and the hazard to cats and dogs is undocumented beyond those values. Plant Type is Edible, Herb, Perennial, Shrub. Edibility field: 'Leaves and flowers are used in teas, desserts, fruit salads and jams' -- the leaves and flowers are the parts named. No handling warning or preparation instruction appears on the page. RHS's page carries no toxicity text.
unknowns: Size 72-96 in is NC State's in-ground Dimensions block (6-8 ft); the same page's prose says 2 to 4 feet tall and wide in a pot (24-48 in), so container-grown plants will be much smaller. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in), which differs from NC State at the low end; NC State is used as the anchor.

NC State's Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics lists Broadleaf Evergreen, Deciduous and Semi-evergreen together; its prose says the plant loses its leaves when brought indoors for the winter in a pot, and RHS calls it deciduous. Leaf habit is therefore unresolved and there is no schema field for it.

is_houseplant false: neither source frames lemon verbena as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field reads Edible, Herb, Perennial, Shrub with no Houseplant value, and its Description says 'In zones 8 and higher, it can be grown outdoors. In cold climates, it can be grown in a pot and brought indoors for the winter, where it will lose its leaves.', a cold-climate overwintering practice in which the plant drops its leaves, not indoor culture. RHS's type tags read Conservatory Greenhouse, Shrubs and Herbs - Culinary.
Toxicity rests only on NC State's structured Problems field (cats, dogs, horses); no severity, principle, part or symptoms are given and RHS says nothing, so the actual hazard is undocumented.

NC State's dedicated page title parenthetical reads (Japanese Medlar, Japanese Plum, Loquat), and its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, in the same order. RHS's page title reads Eriobotrya japonica (F) | Japanese loquat, the subtitle beneath its H1 reads Japanese loquat, and its Other common names line reads Japanese medlar, Japanese plum, loquat, nispero. records.toxicity_detail: NC State: the Plant Type field renders Edible, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Tree, and the Problems field reads Poisonous to Humans. The page's summary line reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Its Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: If large quantities of cracked seed pits are eaten: weakness, vomiting, labored breathing, twitching, stupor, convulsions. A low risk for poison exists if one cracks multiple seeds and eats them. The risk is from the kernel pit inside the seed. Large quantities of cracked seeds would need to be eaten for toxicity to occur. Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycoside. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Seeds. Edibility (same page): Fruit flesh is edible raw or in jams, jellies, pies, syrups, and marmalades. NC State's Tags list carries #poisonous (unscoped), #edible fruits, #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for horses and #non-toxic for dogs. The cat and dog tags are the only cat/dog evidence, so toxic_to_pets is false, while the seed warning stands for people. RHS (Potentially harmful): Seeds contain toxins so these should be removed if you are considering eating the fruit; usually grown as an ornamental shrub. Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers. That Pets line names no animal, so RHS is not used for toxic_to_pets. RHS does not dispute that the fruit is edible: its description reads Fruit 4cm, apricot-yellow, edible but seldom ripening in most of UK.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State: the plant usually does not fruit in NC; if the temperature falls below 28 degrees F, blooms or fruit likely will not survive, while the tree itself can survive in temps down to about 10 degrees F.
unknowns: Taxonomy: GBIF and POWO now treat Eriobotrya japonica as Rhaphiolepis bibas. Neither is an admissible source, so this is not cited; RHS (Name Status Correct) and NC State both use Eriobotrya japonica. NC State lists Crataegus bibas and Mespilus japonica as previously known as. Nothing was taken from the landed Rhaphiolepis indica (Indian Hawthorn) record.
The MoBot Plant Finder page and the UF/IFAS EDIS ST235 publication could not be loaded in this session (connection errors), so nothing is taken from them.

toxic_to_pets is false only from NC State's explicit #non-toxic for cats and #non-toxic for dogs tags; the same Tags list also carries #poisonous (unscoped) and #non-toxic for horses, and the page's human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block names the seeds (Cyanogenic glycoside, Low severity). RHS's Potentially harmful field says 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten', naming no animal, so it supports neither value.

Edibility is conditional: NC State says fruit flesh is edible raw or in jams, jellies, pies, syrups, and marmalades, and its Poison Part is Seeds, with symptoms only if large quantities of cracked seed pits are eaten. RHS agrees the fruit is edible (its description reads 'Fruit 4cm, apricot-yellow, edible but seldom ripening in most of UK') and says the seeds contain toxins and should be removed if you are considering eating the fruit; its 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten' line sits under 'Pets:'. Clemson says to consume the raw fruit or process it into jellies, jams, preserves, and pies.

chill_damage_f 28 is NC State's threshold for blooms and fruit only; the tree survives to about 10 F per NC State. Clemson gives 12 F tree hardiness and flower damage at 27 F. NC State's USDA zones are 8a-11b. NC State says it usually does not fruit in NC.

water_regime null: NC State gives Moist/Occasionally Dry as a soil drainage field, not a watering statement; Clemson only says to water regularly during drought and avoid prolonged dry stress. Dry-down, check depth and day intervals not stated.
Light: NC State lists full sun and Partial Shade (mapped to part_shade); RHS says full sun; Clemson says full sun to part shade. direct_sun_hours_max null since no species prose gives an hour limit.

Size: RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres and Max Spread 4-8 metres (157-315 in), differing from NC State's 10-25 ft; NC State's Dimensions anchor used. Clemson says typically 10 to 20 feet tall, up to 30 feet.

Fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) is NC State's and Clemson's named disease problem. Fertilizer: Clemson says fertilize by soil test and avoid excess nitrogen; no strength or interval stated. Temperature day/night ranges, humidity and indoor light not stated by admissible sources.
Soil drainage moderate follows NC State's Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry field with clay, loam and sand textures; it is not fast. Clemson says only well-drained.

unknowns: Two admissible pages are dedicated to this species. Every landed value rests on NC State's Ocimum tenuiflorum page, except the spread (see the size line). records.toxicity_detail: NC State has no Poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag and no Edibility field for Glycine max; its Plant Type field lists three values (Annual, Edible, Warm Season Vegetable) and its tags read "#edible garden #cover crop #edible seeds #summer annual #vegetable #nitrogen fixation #cover crop-summer". NC State's harvest prose: for fresh seed (edamame) harvest the pods when the seeds are plump and the pod is just beginning to lose its fresh green color; for dry beans allow the pods to mature and dry on the plant, with additional post-harvest drying possibly necessary. RHS (the soya-bean growing guide, not a poison listing, and naming no animal) says the beans "must always be cooked before eating, to get rid of any natural toxins"; edamame "must be boiled for at least ten minutes to destroy their natural toxins" whether shelled or cooked in the pods (then shelled); and mature soya beans must be cooked thoroughly to remove any natural toxins. NC State states no such cooking requirement; this difference between the two sources is disclosed here. No admissible source names cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets stays null.

soil_drainage moderate rests on RHS's profile Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained'. MoBot's Culture reads 'Best in loose, fertile, moist but well-drained soils in full sun.' (read in a browser by the auditor; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited). NC State's Soil Drainage values are Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, with Clay, Loam (Silt) and Sand textures; that is not fast and does not contradict moderate. RHS's growing guide asks for 'light, free-draining soil', which on its own is ambiguous.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field renders one value, 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', with no Acid band, and RHS's dedicated profile gives pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', accepting acid and alkaline soils, so neither end of NC State's band is landed as a bound (this catalog checks RHS's pH field in both directions). UMD's edamame production chapter gives 'The optimum soil pH for edamame is between 6.0 and 6.5.', an optimum rather than a tolerance limit, which is not landed either.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State's watering sentence 'The plants need regular irrigation, but can tolerate brief periods of drought once established.' and RHS's 'Soya beans are thirsty plants and crop best when watered regularly in dry spells, especially once they start to flower and form pods.'; RHS also says soya beans 'need full sun, heat and plenty of moisture'. Counterpoints, disclosed and not used: NC State's Soil Drainage values are Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry; MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale); UMD's edamame production chapter calls edamame 'a relatively drought-tolerant plant, which tends to respond well to irrigation, especially during pod fill'. The drought clauses are tolerances, not drying-down instructions. No source gives a dry-down target or day interval for this annual crop, so those fields are null.

Temperature, humidity, indoor light, fertilizer and pollinator fields are null: no admissible source gives them for Glycine max. RHS's 20-30C (68-86F) summer range and NC State's 75-85F germination soil temperature are not day/night air-temperature ranges and are not used. NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' is a lower bound, so direct_sun_hours_max is null.

NC State inoculating seed with a nitrogen-fixing inoculant and avoiding very nitrogen-rich soil are planting notes, not soil enums, and are not used for soil_base beyond 'grows readily in most garden soils'.

is_houseplant false: no source frames Glycine max as a houseplant or describes indoor culture; NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible and Warm Season Vegetable, and its prose calls it 'an easy-to-grow vegetable' in the average garden.

Mature size is NC State's structured Dimensions block for Glycine max ('Height: 1 ft. 0 in. - 2 ft. 0 in.', 'Width: 0 ft. 9 in. - 2 ft. 0 in.' = 12-24 in tall, 9-24 in wide), the anchor for a species with its own NC State page; RHS's growing guide agrees ('Most soya bean varieties sold in the UK grow to about 60cm (2ft) tall and are self-supporting.'). records.name_note: The two dedicated pages for this species lead with different names. RHS's page title reads "Symphytum officinale | common comfrey". NC State's page-title parenthetical is an alphabetized list that begins with Black wort, with Comfrey fourth and Common Comfrey fifth. Bare Comfrey is not used: NC State's description calls this plant "One of the many plants called comfrey", and NC State's Symphytum grandiflorum page lists Comfrey first. records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Symphytum officinale, "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped; the page carries no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags). Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: "Ingestion can lead to liver damage, lung damage, and cancer. Considered possibly safe to use externally." Poison Toxic Principle: Pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems (every part listed). Same page, Plant Type: Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Wildflower; Problems: Weedy; tags include #medicinal and #weedy. The description says of its long medicinal use that "it is no longer deemed as safe for consumption", so no edibility is recorded. RHS (separate source, Potentially harmful): "Harmful if eaten repeatedly. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "Pets (rabbits, rodents): Harmful if eaten repeatedly"; it names no cats or dogs. The sources differ in scope: RHS qualifies the eating hazard with "repeatedly" where NC State's symptom line has no such qualifier, and RHS says to wear gloves when handling where NC State lists Causes Contact Dermatitis: No and calls external use possibly safe.
unknowns: Only NC State and RHS have dedicated pages for this exact species that could be read. The Missouri Botanical Garden page (kempercode b472) could not be fetched (ConnectError), so MoBot contributes nothing. Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA were not searched for a dedicated page.

Cultivation cautions (not size): NC State lists Problems: Weedy and says it "easily spreads and will sprout from any root pieces left behind from removal"; it suggests large containers to control spread. RHS says growth can be vigorous with potential to become a nuisance.

records.name_note: Hardy Kiwi is the name used by both pages with a dedicated page for this taxon. NC State's page-title parenthetical is an alphabetized list that begins with Bower actinidia and includes Hardy Kiwi, and its description opens with 'Hardy kiwi'. RHS's page for this taxon (titled 'Actinidia arguta [2] (f/F)') carries 'hardy kiwi' as its common name and separately lists other common names, which include kokuwa, Siberian gooseberry, tara vine and yang-tao.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, so no toxicity severity is recorded. Its Plant Type field lists Edible and Vine. Its Edibility field reads 'The fruit is edible, the sap can be extracted to drink.' and its description says the fruit does not need peeling, making the entire fruit edible. Its only mention of cats is a pest note about catnip-like scent and digging damage to foliage and roots, which is not a toxicity statement. Fruiting needs both a male and a female plant.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs as at risk. NC State has no Poison block or pet tag; its cat note (catnip-like scent, cats damage foliage and roots while digging) is a pest problem, not toxicity.

mature_height_in left null: NC State's 25-30 ft Height is vine length on a sturdy structure (the page says to grow it on one), and RHS's Max Height of 8-12 metres is likewise a climber's extent. The page also says the vine can grow 30 feet in one year, which is vigor, not mature size. RHS's Max Spread is the open-ended 'wider than 8 metres', so it gives no usable bound.

mature_spread_in 84-240 comes from NC State's species-page Dimensions block, 'Width: 7 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.' (7-20 ft x 12). RHS disagrees: its Max Spread reads 'wider than 8 metres' (more than about 315 in), which lies wholly above NC State's range. Being open-ended, the RHS value sets no bound, so NC State's figure is used as the anchor and the conflict is disclosed here.

Missouri Botanical Garden's page for Actinidia arguta could not be loaded in this session (connection error), so it was not used. No other admissible domain has a dedicated single-species page for this taxon. Penn State Extension's 'Hardy Kiwi in the Home Fruit Planting' treats hardy kiwi as Actinidia arguta and Actinidia kolomikta together; UGA's 'Minor Fruits and Nuts in Georgia' (B992) groups A. arguta with A. kolomikta and A. polygama as the cold-hardy kiwifruit; and RHS's 'How to grow kiwi fruit' guide covers Actinidia deliciosa and Actinidia arguta together. These multi-species pages were not used for any value. RHS also has a second entry for the species, 'Actinidia arguta [3] (m)', which carries the same 'hardy kiwi' subtitle but no growing fields; every RHS value here comes from the '[2] (f/F)' entry.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State ticks Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and the acid and alkaline bands are open-ended. RHS says acid or neutral, which gives no numbers.

water_regime left null: NC State's Moist (paired with Good Drainage) and RHS's 'moist but well-drained' are soil-moisture descriptors, not watering instructions. Root rot is noted as an issue, so keep_moist is not supported.

RHS's page for this taxon is 'Actinidia arguta [2] (f/F)'. Its Position field is Full sun only, while NC State also lists Partial Shade. Partial shade is included from NC State and from the description's 'full sun to partial shade'. RHS's H6 hardiness rating is a UK rating, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.
Edibility is the whole smooth-skinned fruit, eaten unpeeled, plus drinkable sap. Fruiting needs both a male and a female plant. No admissible source flags any poisonous part.

No admissible dedicated page gives humidity, light in foot-candles, temperature ranges, a direct-sun hour figure, fertilizer details or a watering cadence for this species. Penn State Extension's 'Hardy Kiwi in the Home Fruit Planting', a two-species page (Actinidia arguta and A. kolomikta), does give fertilizer guidance: apply it cautiously because hardy kiwi roots burn rather easily; none in the planting year; then 2 ounces of 10-10-10 per plant in the spring of the second year, increased by 2 ounces each year to 8 ounces per plant. It also says to irrigate throughout the season as needed. Because it covers two species and gives an annual per-plant amount with no interval, month list or dilution, it fills no fertilize or water field.

Other plants sold as hardy kiwi (such as Actinidia kolomikta) and Actinidia deliciosa (kiwifruit) are separate taxa. Nothing here is drawn from them, and the Siberian Gooseberry alias on these pages refers to this species.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Loofah, Luffa Sponge, Smooth Luffa, Sponge Gourd) and its order matches the page-title parenthetical, while its Description opens 'Sponge gourd is an annual climbing vine in the cucumber family.' RHS's page title is 'Luffa aegyptiaca | loofah' and its Other common names field reads 'loofah, vegetable sponge'. Sponge Gourd was chosen because NC State's description prose leads with it. NC State gives Luffa cylindrica as the previous name; RHS lists Luffa cylindrica as a misapplied synonym.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS (Botanical Details, 'Potentially harmful') says: 'Harmful if eaten, except young fruit; don't eat if bitter. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling', and for pets: 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten, except young fruit; don't eat if bitter'. RHS names no poisonous part list and no symptom list. NC State has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. NC State's Plant Type values are Annual, Edible, Vegetable, Vine. Edibility is conditional: NC State says young fruits (typically less than 7 inches long and green) can be eaten as squash or fresh cucumber substitute, and seeds can be roasted and eaten; as the fruit matures it becomes fibrous and inedible and is used as a loofah sponge. The sources differ in scope: RHS exempts only young fruit from 'harmful if eaten' (and adds don't eat if bitter), while NC State also lists roasted seeds as edible.
unknowns: mature_height_in left null: NC State's Height 30-50 ft is vine length ('the vines can grow to 30 to 50 feet long'), and RHS's Max Height 2.5-4 metres is a climbing height on support, so neither is the plant's own height.
Spread: NC State Width 12-36 in is used; RHS Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) differs slightly.

Cultivation note: NC State says sponge gourd requires a frost-free growing season of at least four months and warm temperatures for flowering and fruiting; no chill-damage onset temperature is stated, so chill_damage_f is null. NC State zones 8a-11b and RHS H1C are survival/growing ratings, not damage onsets.

Edibility is conditional. NC State: 'Young fruits that are less than 7 inches long can be eaten as squash or fresh cucumber substitute. Seeds can be roasted and eaten.' and 'As the fruit matures, it becomes fibrous and inedible, but ideal for use as a loofah, or scrubbing sponge.' RHS: 'Harmful if eaten, except young fruit; don't eat if bitter. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on RHS's 'Pets (dogs, cats)' line; it is scoped to eating, with young fruit excepted. RHS's Luffa operculata page renders the identical Potentially harmful text, so the wording is not specific to this species. Neither RHS nor NC State gives a symptom list, and MoBot's Luffa aegyptiaca page, read in a browser by the auditor, has no toxicity text. NC State has no pet tag and no Poison block.
Soil pH: NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral, so both pH bounds are null.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering statement. NC State's 'well-drained, evenly moist, rich loam' and MoBot's 'Best grown in evenly moist, moderately rich, well-draining loams in full sun.' describe soil. RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' and MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' are both mid-scale and do not support keep_moist. These support soil_drainage moderate, not a watering token. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields are null.

humidity_need null: NC State's '#humidity tolerant' tag and its Resistance To Challenges value Humidity are tolerance traits, not a humidity requirement, and RHS's 'provide high humidity' is part of its under-glass Cultivation sentence, which RHS's Luffa operculata page repeats word for word, so neither is used.
direct_sun_hours_max null: NC State's 'at least 6 hours of full sun' is a minimum, not a maximum.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Vegetable and Vine, its Landscape Location field lists Rock Wall and Vertical Spaces, and it says to sow seeds directly in the garden (starting them indoors only in cooler zones, 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost).

MoBot's dedicated Luffa aegyptiaca page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=364305) fails TLS certificate verification for the pipeline's clients, so the quote checker cannot read it; it was read in a browser by the auditor and is not cited. It gives 'Common Name: sponge gourd', 'Sun: Full sun', 'Water: Medium', 'Height: 30.00 to 50.00 feet' and 'Spread: 1.00 to 3.00 feet'; its Noteworthy Characteristics say "Vines can reach 30-50' long and require 1-3' of spacing."; it has no toxicity text. The Clemson and UF/IFAS Luffa pages found are genus-level, so they were not used. No page read gives a fertilizer schedule, a growing-temperature range or a light-intensity figure (RHS's 'Sow seeds at 21-24°C in early spring' is a germination temperature), so those fields are null.
Light: NC State and RHS agree on full sun, so outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only.
